source_excerpt: DHARASHIV: At the Kasbe Todwale market, eager vendors lay out Diwali treats: baskets of spicy chivda, grated coconut laddoos and the glazed rows of balushahi mithai. There are stalls of sequinned frocks and saris, mounds of luminous glass bangles, brass cattle bells and even farm tools and seeds.But the market is still, like a film set waiting for actors to enter. Even though the festive season is approaching, only a handful of customers loiter at this weekly bazaar in Dharashiv, which caters to as many as 10 villages.Pooja Pawar, a farm labourer, has not found work for over two weeks. With the El Nino factor resulting in a rain shortfall, the drought covers 85% of the state (304 of 358 talukas). In Dharashiv, which had a 41% rain deficit, the drought has ravaged cotton and soyabean crops, the mainstay of the local economy.Till a few months ago, the market was so packed that there was barely space to move. But its customers are mainly farmers and farm labourers. With their crops destroyed and no income, their purchasing power has plummeted.Muzaffar Alam Todwada, who sells Diwali sweets and savouries, has earned only Rs 1,500, although the market day is almost over. Even the children are not demanding clothes, sweets or firecrackers because no one has them,â he says.What do the people here think of the stateâs announcement of pre-Diwali relief of Rs 5,000 each for drought-affected farmers? âGiven how much we have lost, it is almost a joke. But things are so bad that anything will help,â says Gadkari.For Rishikesh Thombre, who has a stall selling saris, the poor Dussehra sales were an indicator of the flattened demand for Diwali. âPeople are only replacing clothes which are torn or the children have outgrown.
